paper_metadata.title: Quantum Financial Modeling on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Hardware: Random Walks using Approximate Quantum Counting

summary: The paper introduces several approximate quantum counting circuits (arc counter, arc walk, and random jump) for NISQ‑era quantum walk simulations. On an 11‑qubit trapped‑ion device using 6‑qubit counter registers, traditional binary counting fails after ~2 steps due to noise, while arc‑based approximate counters maintain monotonically increasing behavior over up to 10 steps. Simulated mid‑measurement experiments show a Zeno‑like effect where the average walk distance drops from 35.6 (no measurements) to 5.7 when measured every step.

experiments.description: Binary counter and arc counter circuits run on an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU, compared against ideal and noisy simulations for counting/position tracking in quantum walks.

algorithm.variant: binary counter and arc counter circuits for quantum walk position tracking

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary counter uses positional binary representation; arc counter uses rotation/arc encoding with one qubit per binary digit and decreasing rotation rate for higher-order qubits.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Track position in a quantum walk / random walk by incrementing a counter register over repeated steps.

problem_instance.description: Counting/position-tracking benchmark for quantum walk steps; results reported for up to 10 steps in tables and figures.

dataset_specification.description: Ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and QPU runs; 6-qubit counting registers in simulation and 11 trapped-ion qubits on hardware.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average distance traveled after n steps; ideal simulation uses 1000 shots per circuit, QPU results compared to ideal and noisy simulation.

speedup_claims.conditions: NISQ-era hardware; focus is on reduced entangling-gate count and robustness rather than asymptotic speedup
speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic quantum advantage is claimed; the paper emphasizes practical robustness and lower 2-qubit gate usage.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No asymptotic speedup claimed; experiments only demonstrate that approximate counting circuits (arc counter) are more noise‑robust than exact binary counters on a small 11‑qubit trapped‑ion device.
limiting_factors: No algorithmic speedup over classical simulation
Task easily simulable on classical hardware
Focus is noise robustness rather than computational complexity improvement

notes: 11 trapped-ion qubits are explicitly reported for the QPU experiment.
Circuit depth is not explicitly reported; only gate-count comparisons and qualitative gate-efficiency discussion are given.
No asymptotic speedup is claimed; the paper emphasizes NISQ robustness and reduced entangling-gate count instead.
The authors explicitly state that arc counter circuits have no physical quantum advantage and can be easily simulated classically.
The experiment compares circuit robustness rather than quantum vs classical computational performance.

experiments.description: Arc walk counter circuit with a Hadamard coin, evaluated in ideal simulation for monotonic position tracking over 10-15 steps.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Hadamard coin controls a set of qubit rotations with angles decreasing by powers of two across the counter register.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Simulate a quantum walk / random walk with approximate counting-based position updates.

speedup_claims.caveats: No classical baseline or speedup claim is reported; the result is used to show the effect of mid-measurement on average distance traveled.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No complexity advantage claimed; circuit intended as an approximate counting mechanism for NISQ quantum walk modeling.

notes: The paper reports ideal simulation results and does not name a QPU for this experiment, so simulator_statevector is inferred.

problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Classical random selection of target qubits; optional reversal and superposition via post-processing for two-way walks.

experiments.description: Random jump circuit with cascading disjunction gates evaluated in ideal simulation for position propagation in approximate quantum counting.

algorithm.details: Random target-qubit flips combined with Boolean disjunction propagation to higher-order qubits using Toffoli-based circuits with ancilla reset.

Produces stronger monotonic growth of average position compared with random jump without cascading disjunction (Figure 15).

experiments.description: Mid‑measurement quantum walk simulation demonstrating a quantum Zeno‑like effect using approximate counting circuits.

algorithm.variant: arc counter walk with mid‑circuit measurement

key_results: Simulated 20‑step walks with different measurement frequencies.
Average positions reached: 35.6 (no mid‑measurement), 14.3 (measurement every 7 steps), 5.7 (measurement every step).
Demonstrates that increased measurement frequency suppresses large walk displacements (Figure 18).
